Chapter 6: The Unchosen Burden—Consent and the Ethics of Creation.
There’s a quiet truth that slips by in everyday life—a truth that rarely gets spoken out loud. None of us ever asked to be born. That decision? It’s always made for us, by someone else, long before we’re even aware of the world. For most people, it’s just something they never really think about. It fades into the background, overshadowed by the busyness of living.
But if you ever stop and really consider what it means—especially when you think about the possibility of harm—you can’t help but notice just how strange it is. The fact that we have no say in our own beginning suddenly feels impossible to ignore.
Imagine this: a young adult, sitting alone after a rough day, replaying the highs and lows that have shaped who they are. There are memories of laughter, sure, but also moments when pain felt almost too much to bear. In a rare moment of honesty, they might wonder, “If I could have chosen—would I have picked this life?” It’s a question that lingers, uncomfortable and unanswerable, because that choice was never theirs to begin with.
And that’s not just some small detail. It cuts right to the heart of the matter. When someone is brought into existence, they face all the risks and hardships that life can throw at them—yet they never agreed to take that on. The decision belongs to parents, or to society, but the consequences? Those are carried by the person who never got a vote.
Most of us don’t dwell on this. It’s easier to look on the bright side, to focus on the joys or simply believe that life is always a blessing. But the truth is, whenever someone new comes into the world, it’s a roll of the dice. And the one who pays the price is the one who never got to choose.
Now, some people try to make sense of this by saying, “Well, most folks end up happy to be alive.” But that doesn’t quite answer the real question. Just because people can adapt or find meaning doesn’t change the fact that they were never given the option in the first place. The impact of not being able to consent—it’s real, even if we rarely talk about it.
Picture our young adult, closing their eyes as this all sinks in. It’s not about blaming anyone, or wishing things were different. Instead, it’s about facing the reality that creating a life is a serious responsibility. The lack of consent isn’t just a technicality—it changes everything about the ethics of bringing someone new into the world. And maybe, it’s something we should all think about a little more deeply.
